short: An experiment where some real users get version A and others get version B at the same time. You compare a metric to see which version works better.
How an app reads and writes its data: which queries, by which keys, how often, and how fast the answer must be.
Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability: the four promises a database transaction makes.
Short for acknowledgement. A message a consumer sends to say "I am done with this one", so the broker can stop tracking it.
A protocol that lets software prove it controls a domain and get or renew a certificate with no human involved. Let's Encrypt uses it.
The bank that processes card payments for a merchant. It sends each payment to the card network and collects the money for the merchant.
A follow-up task from a postmortem, such as adding an alert or a safety check. A good one has an owner, a priority and a due date.
A design pattern where a small class implements the interface your code expects by calling another API, often a vendor's. Vendor details stay inside it.
The private view of memory that each process gets. Every address the program sees is virtual; the OS and hardware map it to real RAM. This is called virtual memory.
Short for "architecture decision record". A one- or two-page note, kept with the code, that records one decision, why it was made and what it costs.
A shared Markdown file of project instructions for coding agents, like a README for agents. Many tools read it, and the file closest to the code being changed wins.
What happens when people get so many alerts, most of them useless, that they start to ignore or miss the real ones.
How long a stream processor keeps a window after the watermark passes the window's end. Events for that window arriving in that time still update the result. In Flink it is 0 by default.
A TLS extension where the client lists the protocols it speaks, such as h2 or http/1.1, and the server picks one, with no extra round trip.
An HTTP response header that tells the client the same site is also available another way, for example over HTTP/3 on UDP port 443.
When the problem is not clearly defined. Nobody has decided yet what to build, why, or what "done" means.
A common answer to a problem that looks like a solution but makes things worse. The term was coined by Andrew Koenig.
Announcing the same IP address from many places, so the network sends each user to the nearest one.
A server in front of your services that receives every API request. It does shared jobs such as checking logins, rate limits and sending each request to the right service.
Data you can only add to. Old records are never updated or deleted, so the full history stays.
How much time a problem is worth to you, decided before you design a solution. You then shape the work to fit that time.
The leader confirms a write to the client right away and sends it to followers in the background.
A delivery promise. No message is lost, but some may be handled more than once.
A delivery promise. No message is handled twice, but some may be lost.
An atomic operation happens completely or not at all. If it fails partway, every part of it is undone.
Checking who a user or service is, for example with a password, a second factor or a login at another provider. It answers "who are you?", not "what may you do?".
The DNS server that holds the real records for a zone, such as example.com. Other servers only cache or point to it.
A game server that owns the true state of the game. Players' games only send inputs, and the server decides what really happened, which makes cheating harder.
Checking what a known user or service may do, such as reading one order or deleting a project. It must run on the server for every request.
A database feature that gives each new row the next number in a counter, like 1, 2, 3. One database owns the counter.
Adding or removing servers automatically as traffic goes up or down.
The share of time, or of requests, in which a system works for its users. It is usually written as a percentage, such as 99.9% over a month.
A sorted tree of fixed-size pages on disk. The database changes pages in place. Most SQL databases use it for indexes.
A quick, rough calculation with round numbers and written assumptions. It tells you the size of a problem before you design for it.
A small backend built for one user interface, such as the mobile app. It shapes and combines data for that client, and the UI team usually owns it.
A job that fills in or fixes data in rows that already exist, for example copying a value into a new column. On a live database, run it in small batches.
Waiting longer after each failed try, for example 1, 2, then 4 seconds.
A way for a slow part of a system to make faster parts slow down or wait, instead of being flooded.
A file format many US banks use to send account balances and transactions to their customers, usually every day.
The time you wait at each rollout stage, watching metrics, before sending a change wider.
How much data a network link can carry per second, usually in bits per second, such as 1 Gbit/s.
At Amazon, a trained interviewer who joins a hiring loop as a neutral third party and helps lead the decision, so no single person decides alone.
A full copy of a database's data files, taken while it runs. Point-in-time recovery starts from it and replays the change log on top.
Grouping many items into one operation, such as one network call or one disk write, so they share its fixed cost. It raises throughput but an item may wait for others to join.
An interview question about what you really did in the past, such as "Tell me about a time you missed a deadline." It differs from a hypothetical question, such as "What would you do if…?"
The stretch of time one invoice covers, for example 1 to 30 November. Usage counts toward the period in which it happened.
Finding a problem by splitting the search space in half again and again, for example by time, version or region.
A postmortem that looks for the causes in systems and processes, not for a person to blame, so people share what really happened.
How many users or systems a failure can reach. A small blast radius means a bad change hurts only a few.
A small data structure that says a key is surely not in a set, or may be in it. It is never wrong about "not".
A classic ranking function for keyword search. It scores documents by how well their exact words match the words in the query.
A bug where an API takes an object ID from the client, like an order number, and uses it without checking that the caller may see that object.
Well-known, mature tools like Postgres or cron. Not bad, just old enough that their limits and failure modes are well understood. The idea is from Dan McKinley's essay "Choose Boring Technology".
The CPU guesses which way an if or a loop will go and starts work on that path early. A wrong guess throws that work away and costs time.
A change to an API or data format that makes existing clients fail, such as removing or renaming a field.
A SaaS design that mixes silo and pool, for example a shared app with a separate database for some tenants or services.
The file a build produces and you deploy, such as a container image, a JAR or an app bundle. Build it once and deploy that same file everywhere.
How fast a service spends its error budget. At burn rate 1, the budget runs out exactly at the end of the SLO window.
A caching pattern where the app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and writes the value into the cache itself.
Putting a version or content hash in a file name, so each new version gets a new URL and caches can never serve an old copy.
The share of requests a cache answers from its own copy. A ratio of 0.9 means the cache answers 9 of 10 requests from its own copy.
Removing or updating a cached value when the source data changes, so readers do not see old data.
The value a cache uses to decide which requests share one stored copy. In HTTP it is at least the method and the URL.
The fixed-size block that a CPU cache moves to and from memory, usually 64 bytes. When you read one byte, the CPU loads the whole line that holds it.
A cache hit is when the data is in the cache. A cache miss is when it is not, so you must read it from the source.
Telling a CDN to drop or mark stale its stored copies, by URL, tag or everything, so the next request fetches a fresh copy.
When a popular cache key expires and many requests miss at once, all loading the same data from the database.
A fast copy of data that is slow or costly to get, kept close to where it is read.
The ISO 20022 XML message for a bank account statement. It holds the opening and closing balances and every entry for the period, often one day.
A small part of the fleet, such as 1% of servers, that gets a change first. You compare it with the rest before going wider.
A proof that during a network partition, a replicated system cannot be both consistent (linearizable) and available. Each cut-off node must choose.
The network of a card brand, such as Visa or Mastercard, that carries payment messages and money between the merchant's bank and the card's bank.
A company document that describes what is expected at each job level, for example scope, impact and how widely you work with others.
If one operation may have caused another, like a reply to a comment, everyone sees them in that order.
A content delivery network. Many data centers around the world that keep copies of your content close to users, so pages load faster and your servers get less traffic.
One account with millions of followers overloads the system. With fan-out on write, each of its posts must be copied into millions of feeds.
A full, independent copy of a workload that serves only some customers. A router sends each customer to its cell, so one failure stays inside one cell.

An organisation that signs certificates after it checks the requester. For most web certificates, it checks that the requester controls the domain. Clients trust a certificate if a trusted certificate authority signed it.
A Linux feature that groups processes and limits what they may use together, such as memory and CPU. Containers use cgroups for their limits.
The list of certificates from a site's certificate up to a trusted root. Each one is signed by the next one up, so the client can check them all.
When a simple change needs edits in many places in the code. It is a sign that a design decision is spread across modules.
Reading every insert, update and delete from a database's change log, and sending them on as events to other systems.
When a cardholder disputes a payment with their card issuer. The money is pulled back from the merchant, often with a fee, and the issuer later decides who is right.
A marker a stream processor puts into the data stream. When the barrier has arrived from all of an operator's inputs, the operator saves its state, so all saved states match one point in the input.
A way to run a saga with no one in charge. Each service listens for events and reacts with its own step.
A public Google dataset of how real Chrome users experience popular websites, including the Core Web Vitals.
Splitting long documents into smaller pieces (chunks) before you index them for search. The size and borders of each piece change what search can find.
A guard around calls to another service. After many failures it stops sending calls for a short time, so the failing service can recover and the caller does not wait.
Splitting code into so many small classes that each one adds very little. You must learn many interfaces to get simple work done.
A Markdown file of project instructions that Claude Code reads at the start of every session, like build commands and team rules.
A ledger account that holds money only while it is on the way, for example between a payment and its payout. When every step finishes, it should go back to zero.
The player's game shows the result of their own input at once, as a guess, instead of waiting for the server. The server's answer later confirms or corrects it.
Building a page in the browser with JavaScript that changes the DOM. The server sends little HTML and a script bundle.
The difference between the times shown by two clocks at the same moment, for example on two servers.
A DNS record that makes one name an alias for another name. The resolver then looks up the other name.
A part of the code that changes often and is hard to work with. Tools like CodeScene suggest improving hotspots first, because you pay the extra cost on every change.
Cutting a JavaScript bundle into smaller pieces, so the browser downloads only the code the first view needs and loads the rest later.
An AI tool that works in a loop on your code. It reads files, edits them, runs commands and checks the results until the task looks done.
How much information you must hold in your head at once to understand or change a piece of code.
How strongly the parts inside one module belong together. High cohesion means the parts serve one purpose and tend to change together.
In Raft, the position of the last log entry known to be stored on a majority of servers. Entries up to it are safe to apply.
In Spanner, the short wait after a write picks its timestamp. Nobody can see the data until that timestamp has surely passed, given the clock uncertainty.
Background work in an LSM-tree that merges several SSTables into one and drops old versions and deleted keys.
One atomic CPU step: if a variable still holds the value you expect, set it to a new value and report success. Otherwise change nothing and report failure.
A new action that undoes the effect of an earlier step, such as a refund for a charge. It does not erase the first step.
A model by Steve McConnell. Early estimates can be far too high or too low. The possible error shrinks only as the team makes decisions and removes unknowns. It shows the best case.
Noticing only the facts that fit what you already believe, and missing the facts that do not.
Rules that make a sender slow down when the network looks overloaded, for example when packets get lost, so the network does not collapse.
A vocabulary for kinds of coupling. For example, two functions that must agree on the order of values in a list are connascent by position.
Stopping new requests to a server you are removing, while letting the requests it already has finish.
A QUIC feature that keeps a connection alive when the client's IP address or port changes, because the connection is found by an ID, not by its address.

A set of open database connections that are reused, so a new connection is not opened for every request. The pool can live inside the app. Or a separate program, a connection pooler such as PgBouncer, can keep one pool that many apps share.
A way for a group of machines to agree on one value or one order of changes, even when some of them fail. Raft and Paxos are examples.
A promise about what reads can see after writes in a system with many copies of the data, from strong to weak.
A way to map keys to servers so that adding or removing one server moves only a small share of the keys.
A set of Kafka consumers that share the work of reading a topic. Each partition is read by only one member of the group at a time.
Choosing and arranging everything a model sees for one request, such as instructions, examples, documents, tool results and history, so the useful tokens fit and the noise stays out.
The drop in a model's accuracy and recall as its context window fills with more tokens. A long prompt can hide the one fact the model needs.
The kernel stops one thread, saves its registers, and starts another. It lets many threads share one CPU, but each switch costs time.
Everything a model can see at once, such as messages, files it read and command output. It has a size limit, and quality drops as it fills.
Building software so that any version that passes the pipeline can be released to production at any time. A person still chooses when to deploy.
Every change that passes the automated pipeline goes to production on its own, with no human step.
Continuous integration. A system that builds the code and runs the tests and other checks on every change, before it is merged.
A test that checks two services agree on the requests and responses between them, without starting both services together.
One of several conditions that together caused an incident. Many teams list contributing factors instead of looking for one single root cause.
Melvin Conway's 1968 idea that organisations which design systems produce designs that copy their own communication structure.
Three numbers from Google that describe how a page feels to real users: LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness and CLS for visual stability.
An ID attached to one request and passed to every service it touches, so you can find all of its logs and spans. A trace ID is one kind.
What you lose for each week a piece of work is not done. It combines how valuable the work is with how urgent it is, so you can rank features and cleanup work together.
How strongly one module depends on another. With strong coupling, a change in one module forces changes in the other. Stevens, Myers and Constantine described it in a 1974 paper.
Using one model to change data and a different model, often a different store, to read it. Powerful for some parts of a system, but it adds complexity and lag.
When a program crashes, restarts, hits the same problem and crashes again, over and over.
The steps a browser takes to turn HTML, CSS and JavaScript into pixels: build the DOM and CSSOM, make the render tree, do layout, then paint.
A piece of code that reads or changes shared data. Only one thread may run it at a time, or the data can break.
A score for how much content on a page moves without the user asking for it. Good is 0.1 or less.
A way to page through a list where each answer gives an opaque token, the cursor. The client sends it back to get the items after that point.
A public ID for one known security flaw, like CVE-2021-44228. Scanners use these IDs to tell you which of your package versions are affected.
The number of different people who use a product on a given day.
Running new code on real traffic without letting it change results, so you can see what it would do before you turn it on.
The shape you give your data, such as tables with rows, nested documents, or a graph of nodes and links.
A separate queue for messages that failed too many times, so they stop blocking work and you can inspect them.
Guessing where something is now by assuming it kept its last known speed and direction. Works for cars and ships, but not for players who turn suddenly.
The time by which something must be done. For a request, passing the time left down to every call lets servers drop work nobody waits for.
Two transactions each wait for a lock the other one holds, so neither can go on. The database usually cancels one of them with an error.
A query that says what result you want, not the steps to get it, as in SQL or Cypher. The database chooses the indexes and order.
A design pattern that wraps a function or object to add a step, such as logging or timing, and keeps the same interface. Callers and the wrapped code do not change.
The part of a design discussion where you take one hard piece, such as locking or scaling, and work it out in detail with its trade-offs.
A module with a small, simple interface that hides a lot of work behind it. Unix file I/O is the classic example.
When a TCP receiver waits a short time before confirming data, so it can send fewer confirmations. RFC 9293 limits the wait to under 0.5 seconds.
A replica that applies changes on purpose some time after the primary, for example 1 hour later, so you can stop it before a bad change arrives.
Storing a copy of data where it is read, such as a comment count on the post row, so reads need fewer joins. Every write must now update the copies too.
Passing an object the things it needs, for example through its constructor, instead of letting it create them. It is about wiring, not design direction.
The "D" in SOLID. High-level business code should not depend on low-level details. Both depend on an interface shaped by the high-level code.
The automated steps every change goes through, such as build, test, package and deploy. Each stage runs only if the one before it passed.
Marking a feature, field or API version as old and due for removal, while it still works, so users have time to move off it.
A short written plan for a piece of work, shared before you build it. It lists the goals, the options you considered, and the trade-offs.
A named, well-known answer to a design problem that keeps coming back in a certain situation. It gives a team a shared word and a list of trade-offs, not ready-made code.
Code is deterministic when the same starting state and the same inputs always give exactly the same result, on every machine.
The list of lines added, changed and removed between two versions of code. A pull request shows its diff for review.
A backup that holds everything that changed since the last full backup. To restore, you need that full backup plus the newest differential.
Reading data another transaction has written but not yet committed. That data may still be rolled back.
Saying openly that you disagree with a decision, then fully supporting it once it is made, so the team can move on.
A lock that many servers share, often kept in a store like Redis. Only one server or user can hold it at a time, usually until it expires.
The Domain Name System. A tree of names spread over many name servers, which turns names like www.example.com into IP addresses.
A database that stores records as JSON-like documents with nested fields, such as MongoDB.
A way to record money where every movement has at least two entries, one taking money out of an account and one putting it in, so they always sum to zero.
Writing the same change to two systems in two separate calls, such as a database and a message broker. A crash in between leaves them out of step.
How likely it is that data, once saved, stays saved and is not lost. It is different from availability, which is whether you can reach the data right now.
One CDN data center near users. It answers requests from its own cache and asks the origin server only when it has no fresh copy.
How long a Raft follower waits without hearing from a leader before it starts an election. Each server picks it at random.
A list of numbers (a vector) that a model makes from a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning get vectors that are close together, so you can search by meaning.
A test that runs the whole system the way a user does, for example by clicking through a checkout in a real browser.
What a customer is allowed to use because of their plan or contract, for example "Pro accounts can export to PDF".
Drawing other players smoothly between the last two real server updates. They appear a little in the past, often about 100 ms, but based only on real positions.
The amount of failure an SLO allows, which is 100% minus the SLO. A 99.9% SLO gives a budget of 0.1% of requests.
An HTTP response header with a short ID for one version of the content. A client sends it back to ask "has this changed?" and may get a 304 Not Modified answer.
A repeatable test for an LLM feature. It is a set of test cases, a grader that scores each output, and a score you track over time.
The data passed to a feature flag check, such as user ID, plan or country, that the flag's rules use to decide the answer.
The time an event really happened, on the device that produced it. Stream processors use it to put events in the right window, even when they arrive late.
Copies or services may disagree for a while after a change. If no new changes come in, they all end up with the same, latest value.
Removing keys from a cache when it is full, for example the least recently used ones, to make room for new data.
A promise that each message is handled once and only once. In practice it usually means at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent handler.
Making a breaking change in steps. First add the new thing next to the old, then move every user over, then remove the old thing.
A guarantee that if transaction T1 commits before T2 starts, T1 gets the smaller timestamp. Spanner's paper treats it as the same as linearizability.
Stopping quickly at the first sign of a problem, with a clear error, instead of waiting or carrying on in a bad state.
When a check breaks, letting traffic through instead of blocking it, so the check itself does not cause an outage.
Making a follower the new leader when the old leader stops working, and sending writes to it.
Eight false beliefs that designers of distributed systems often hold, such as "the network is reliable" and "latency is zero". First written down at Sun in the 1990s.
A second way to get an answer or do a job, used when the normal way fails or is not available. Fallback code that rarely runs is hard to test, so it can fail when you need it.
When threads on different cores write to different variables that sit in the same cache line. The cores keep taking the line from each other, so the code slows down even though no data is shared.
The system stores each new item once. When a reader asks, it fetches recent items from every source they follow and merges them, as in a feed. Writes are cheap, but every read does more work.

When something new is created, the system copies it (or its ID) at once into a ready-made list for every reader, such as every follower's feed. Reads are fast, but one item for a huge audience means millions of writes.
One request that calls many servers or services at once, then waits for their answers. In feeds and messaging, it also means copying one message to many receivers (see fan-out on write).
A switch read at runtime that turns a piece of code on or off, for some or all users, without a new deploy.
A number that grows each time a lock is given out. Storage rejects writes with an older number, so a client whose lock expired cannot overwrite newer data.
Putting a few worked examples of input and the output you want into the prompt, so the model copies their format and style. With no examples, it is called zero-shot.
Performance numbers collected from all the real users who visit a page, on their own devices and networks.
First in, first out. Items are handled in the order they arrived. LIFO (last in, first out) handles the newest item first.
A small number the kernel gives your process for each open file, socket or pipe. Each process may hold only a limited number at once.
Training an existing model further on your own examples, so its weights change. It shapes how the model behaves, but facts stored in weights are hard to update or trace to a source.
A function you can treat like any other value. You can store it in a variable, pass it to another function or return it.
A rate limit that counts requests in fixed blocks of time, like each calendar minute, and resets the count when a block ends.
Old feature flags that stay in the code after their job is done. Each one adds branches to test and a switch that can be flipped by mistake.
A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code, often because of timing, order or shared state.
A sale of limited stock that starts at a set time, so a very large crowd arrives within minutes.
A number type that stores values as binary fractions. It is fast but not exact for many decimals, like 0.1, so it must not hold money.
A way for a receiver to tell the sender how much more data it can take right now, so a fast sender does not overflow a slow reader.
A 1985 proof by Fischer, Lynch and Paterson. In an asynchronous system, no consensus protocol is sure to finish if even one process may be faulty.
An on-call rotation split between teams in far-apart time zones, so each team covers its own daytime and nobody works at night.
A database copy that only takes changes from the leader. It can answer reads, but it may be a little behind.
A column whose value must match a row in another table, such as order_items.order_id pointing to orders.id. The database rejects values with no match.
A system call that waits until a file's changed data is stored on the disk. Without it, written data may sit only in RAM and be lost on a power cut.
A backoff rule where each wait is a random time between zero and the capped backoff, min(cap, base × 2^n). It spreads retries evenly over that whole window.
Something a user can do with the system, such as "search for events" or "book a seat".
Converting money from one currency to another. The rate and fees used can make the amount you receive differ from the amount you expected.
A planned practice session where a team causes or acts out a failure on purpose, to test its systems and its incident response.
The language runtime frees memory that the program no longer uses. In many runtimes this can pause the program for a short time.
A short pattern that matches file paths. For example, src/**/*.ts matches every TypeScript file under the src folder.
Four things to measure for any service: latency, traffic, errors and saturation (how full it is).
The part of throughput that is handled without errors and in time to be useful.
Still serving users when part of the system fails, with less, for example a page without recommendations, instead of failing the whole request.
A database that stores nodes and the links between them, such as Neo4j. It is good at following many hops of links.
A query language for APIs. The client asks for exactly the fields it needs, often from many resources in one request.
When a database writes the commit records of several transactions to disk with one flush, so they share the cost of that flush.
A framework for calls between services. A client calls a method on a remote server as if it were local, with the contract written in Protocol Buffers.
When a language model writes text that is false, or that does not match the context it was given, as if it were a fact.
Lamport's rule for ordering events without clocks. Event a happens-before b if they are in one process and a comes first, if a sends a message that b receives, or through a chain of these.
The CPU notices a pattern in your memory reads, such as walking an array, and loads the next cache lines before your code asks for them.
When one lost or slow item at the front of a line holds back everything behind it, even items that are ready.

An automatic test of whether a server or service is working. Load balancers use it to stop sending traffic to failing servers. Deploys use it too. For example, a deploy watches the error rate to decide whether to continue or roll back.
A small message sent again and again to say "I am still alive". If heartbeats stop, others assume the sender has failed.
Sending a backup copy of a request to another replica when the first has not answered after a short delay, then using whichever answer comes first.
A group that reads all the written interview feedback on a candidate and decides whether to hire, instead of the interviewers deciding one by one.
The main feed a user sees when they open a social app, made of posts from the accounts they follow, and sometimes recommended posts.
Handling more load by adding more machines that share the work. It avoids the size limit of one machine, and, if built for it, one machine can fail without taking the service down.
Card input fields served by the payment processor inside your page, so the card number goes straight to the processor and never reaches your servers.
A ledger account that appears in a large share of transactions, so many writes wait on the same row.
A single cache or database key that gets a very large share of all reads or writes.
A single database row that very many transactions update at once, such as the stock of a flash-sale product. They wait in line for its lock.
The header compression format of HTTP/2. Both sides keep tables of headers they have seen, so a repeated header can be sent as a small number. HTTP/3 uses a similar format, QPACK.
A response header that tells the browser to use only HTTPS for a site for a set time, and not to let users click through certificate errors.
The HTTP status code a server returns when a client has sent too many requests in a given time.
A timestamp that follows the happens-before order like a Lamport clock, but stays close to real clock time. It fits in 64 bits.
Running keyword search and vector search for the same query and merging the two result lists, so you get both exact matches and matches by meaning.
Running JavaScript in the browser to make server-rendered HTML interactive. Until it finishes, the page can look ready but not respond.
A guess about the cause of a problem that a test can prove wrong, for example "the new pool size is too small".
A signed JWT from an OpenID Connect provider that says who logged in. The app must check its issuer, audience, expiry and, in most cases, its signature.
A unique id the client sends with a request, so the server can spot a repeat and return the saved result.
An action is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once.
A backup that cannot be changed or deleted until a set retention time ends. In its strictest mode, not even an admin can delete it.
A table where a consumer saves the IDs of events it has already handled, so it can skip duplicates.
The person who leads an incident. They hold the overall picture and give out the work, but do not fix things themselves.
A backup that holds only what changed since the previous backup. To restore, you need it and every earlier backup it builds on.
Giving one module sole knowledge of a design decision, such as a data format, so other modules do not depend on it. David Parnas made it famous in a 1972 paper.
When one design decision, such as a file format, is known by several modules. If it changes, all of them must change.
Dan McKinley's idea that a company can afford only a few new or unusual technologies, about three, because each one brings unknown problems.
A test that checks that a few parts work together, for example your code with a real database.
How long a page takes to show a visible response after a click, tap or key press. It reports the slowest one on the page, ignoring a few outliers. Good is 200 ms or less.
The "I" in SOLID. Keep interfaces small, so a caller does not depend on methods it never uses.
A map from each term to the list of documents that contain it, like the index at the back of a book. Search engines use it to find matches without scanning every document.
The number that tells the network which machine a packet is for. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, like 10.0.4.17. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.
A setting that says how much transactions running at the same time can see and change each other's work.
The bank that gave the customer their card. It approves or declines each payment and holds the money during authorization.
Adding a small random amount to each wait, so many clients do not retry at the same moment.
A query step that combines rows from two tables by matching a column, such as orders.user_id = users.id.
A standard way to describe the shape of JSON data, such as which fields exist, their types and which are required. Code can check a document against it.
A compact string that carries claims, such as a user ID and an expiry time, often signed so changes are detected. A signed JWT is not secret, because anyone can read its payload.
Keeping an idle connection open and working. In HTTP, the connection stays open so the next request needs no new handshake. Keep-alive probes or pings check that an idle connection still works.
The core of the operating system. It runs with full access to the hardware and shares the CPU, memory and disks among all programs.
A database that stores each value under a key. You get and put by key. Examples are DynamoDB and Redis.
Data a stream processor remembers between events, split by key, such as a running count per city. Each key's state lives with the task that handles that key.
Paging that asks for the rows after the last row you saw, using its sort values, instead of skipping a number of rows. It stays fast on deep pages.
A quick way to turn off one feature or component everywhere, without a deploy, when it is causing harm.
The date up to which a model's knowledge is most complete and reliable. It may know little or nothing correct about later events.
Performance numbers from loading a page in a controlled setup, with one device and one network. Repeatable, but not what real users get.
The game server rewinds other players to where the shooter saw them, checks the hit there, then moves them back. Shots hit where you aimed despite delay.
A counter on each process that goes up with every event and jumps past any counter it receives in a message. If a happens-before b, a gets the smaller number.
The time from when the user starts loading a page until the largest image, text block or video in view is shown. Good is 2.5 seconds or less.
A rule for conflicting writes: keep the one with the biggest timestamp and drop the rest. With skewed clocks, it can silently drop the newer write.
How long one operation or request takes, from start to answer. Usually measured in milliseconds (ms) or smaller units.
The transport layer of a network (TCP and UDP). A layer 4 load balancer sees connections and ports, not HTTP requests.
The application layer of a network, such as HTTP. A layer 7 load balancer reads each request and can route by path or header.
Loading a resource, such as an image or a piece of code, only when it is about to be needed instead of at the start.
The one database node that accepts writes. It sends every change on to the other copies. Also called the primary.
Amazon's public list of 16 principles it says it uses every day, such as Ownership and Dive Deep. Its interviewers judge every candidate against them.
A rate limit where requests wait in a queue that drains at a fixed rate. When the queue is full, new requests are rejected.
An extra second sometimes added to UTC. Code that assumes time never goes backwards can break when one is added.
A way to add a leap second without a jump. Time servers make each second slightly longer over many hours, so the extra second is spread out.
A lock or role that expires after a set time unless the holder renews it. If the holder crashes, others can take over later.
A load balancing rule that sends each request to the server with the fewest requests still in progress.
Giving each user, service or token only the access it needs for its job, and nothing more. A leak or bug then does less harm.
A record of every movement of money (or points, credits, stock) as entries that are only ever added, never changed. Balances are calculated from it.
A word after it has been normalized for search, for example lowercased and cut to its root. Postgres full-text search stores lexemes.
Google's open-source tool that loads a page in a controlled setup and reports performance and other audits. It gives lab data, not data from real users.
One of the strongest consistency models for a single piece of data. The system acts as if there is one copy of the data, and each operation takes effect at one instant.
A tool that reads your code without running it and flags style problems and common mistakes, the same way every time.
The "L" in SOLID. A subtype must behave the way its supertype promises, so code written for the supertype still works. Matching method types is not enough.
On average, items inside a system = arrival rate × time each item spends inside. For example, 2,000 requests a second × 0.05 s = 100 requests in progress.
Threads keep reacting to each other and retrying, so they stay busy, but none of them makes progress.
Using a language model to grade the output of another model, usually with a written rubric. It is fast and scales, but it has biases you must check.
The unit of text a language model reads and writes. A token can be a word, part of a word, a character or a byte. Providers count cost, limits and speed in tokens.
Large language model. A model trained on a lot of text to predict the next token. It writes likely text, not checked facts.
A service with one address that sits in front of many servers and picks which server gets each connection or request.
Rejecting some requests on purpose when a service is overloaded, so it can keep serving the rest.
A test that sends a lot of fake traffic to a system, to find how much it can handle before it slows down or fails.
A file, such as package-lock.json, that records the exact version of every dependency, so every build installs the same ones.
A backup written as SQL statements or rows, for example by pg_dump. It is portable, but it cannot be combined with the change log for point-in-time recovery.
A branch that stays apart from main for weeks or months. The longer it lives, the bigger and riskier the final merge.
The client sends a request, and the server holds it open until it has new data or a timeout. Then the client sends the next request at once.
Any piece of work on the browser's main thread that takes longer than 50 ms. While it runs, the page cannot respond to the user.
A bug where two transactions read the same value, both change it, and the second write wipes out the first.
A storage design that buffers writes in memory, writes them out as new sorted files, and merges those files later in the background.
The browser thread that runs almost all of a page's JavaScript and handles user input. It can do only one task at a time.
A database that a cloud provider runs for you. It handles setup, patching, backups and failover, so your team does less operations work.
A link where each record on both sides can connect to many on the other, like users and events. In SQL it needs a third table of id pairs.
A database view whose query result is stored like a table. Reads are fast, but the data is only as fresh as the last refresh.
Model Context Protocol, an open standard that connects AI tools to outside systems such as files, databases and other tools.
The sorted table in memory where an LSM-tree collects new writes before it writes them to disk as an SSTable.
A server that holds messages between the services that send them and the services that read them. SQS, RabbitMQ and Kafka are brokers.
A place where one service leaves jobs or messages and another service picks them up later. It lets slow work happen in the background. SQS and RabbitMQ are examples.
A number measured again and again over time, such as requests per second or error rate. Cheap to store and good for graphs and alerts.
Login that needs more than a password, such as a code from an app or a security key. A stolen password alone is then not enough.
A style that builds one application as many small services. Each runs on its own, talks over the network, and can be deployed and scaled on its own.
In web frameworks, a chain of functions that run in turn before a request handler, for example to log or check access. Each one either ends the request or passes control to the next.
The smallest unit of a currency, like paise for rupees or cents for dollars. Storing ₹10.50 as the integer 1050 paise keeps money exact.
An action that stops or reduces harm to users quickly, like a rollback, before you know the exact cause.
A fixed, dated version of a model with a name that does not change, such as one ending in a date. Pinning one keeps behaviour stable until you choose to upgrade.
One application, deployed as one unit, whose code is split into parts with strictly enforced boundaries between business areas.
An application that is built and deployed as one unit. A change to any part means deploying the whole thing.
One repository that holds the code for many projects or services, often owned by different teams.
A clock that only moves forward and cannot be set. Its value means nothing on its own, but the difference between two readings on one machine is a safe way to measure time.
A promise that your reads never go back in time. Once you have seen a change, later reads will not hide it again.
One running system serving many customer organisations (tenants), which share code, servers and often databases.
Sending many separate conversations over one connection at the same time, by cutting them into small labelled pieces and mixing them.

A burn-rate alert that fires only when a long window (for example 1 hour) and a short window (for example 5 minutes) both pass the same threshold. Teams run several such rules with different burn rates: fast ones page, slow ones open a ticket.
A tool makes small changes (mutants) to your code, such as turning > into >=, and runs your tests. If no test fails, your tests missed that bug.
A lock that only one thread can hold at a time. Other threads that want it wait until the holder unlocks it.
TLS where both sides show a certificate, so the server also knows which client is calling. Often used between internal services.
The database keeps several versions of a row, so readers can see an older version while a writer makes a new one.
A TCP rule that holds small writes while earlier data is still unacknowledged, then sends them together. Applications can turn it off with TCP_NODELAY.
Network address translation. A router or gateway swaps private addresses and ports for its own public IP address and ports. This lets many machines share one public address.
New documents become searchable after a short delay, not at once. In Elasticsearch, a refresh makes them visible, by default every second for indices that are being searched.
Caching the answer "this does not exist". In DNS, a resolver remembers that a name has no record, so a record you create later can stay invisible for a while.
A network failure where some nodes cannot reach others, while all of them keep running.
A short way to say availability: 99.9% is "three nines". Each extra nine allows 10 times less downtime.
One user or tenant that puts so much load on shared resources that others sharing them become slow.
A quality the system must have, such as speed, scale, availability or "never sell a seat twice". It shapes how you build, not what users can do.
Something that could reasonably be a goal of a project, but that you chose to leave out. Writing non-goals down keeps the scope from growing.
Designing tables so each fact is stored in one place and other rows point to it by id. Updates touch one row, but reads need joins.
Network Time Protocol. Servers use it to keep their clocks close to a reference time. It makes clocks close, not equal.
Non-uniform memory access. In a server with several CPU sockets, each socket has its own memory. Reading memory attached to another socket is slower than reading local memory.
A standard that lets an app get limited access to an API on a user's behalf, through a token, without the user's password. It is about delegation, not login.
How well you can understand what a system is doing from the data it sends out, such as metrics, logs and traces.
A design pattern where an object tells a list of listeners when something changes, without knowing who they are. Event listeners and event emitters are common forms of it.
The position number of a message in a log, such as a Kafka partition. A consumer saves its offset to remember how far it has read.
The engineer whose turn it is to answer alerts and fix problems, often outside work hours.
A regular private meeting between two people, often a manager or mentor and the person they support. It is for growth, problems and feedback, not status updates.
A decision that is hard or impossible to undo, so it deserves a slow, careful process. Jeff Bezos used the term in his 2015 shareholder letter.

The part of the Linux kernel that ends a process when memory runs out and cannot be freed. In a container, it runs when the container reaches its memory limit and the kernel cannot free enough memory.
The "O" in SOLID. A module should be open for extension and closed for modification, so new behaviour comes from new code, not edits to working code.
A standard file format that describes an HTTP API, its endpoints, fields and errors. Tools use the file to make docs, client code and tests.
An open specification for a vendor-neutral API for checking feature flags. A provider connects it to the flag tool you use.
A login layer on top of OAuth 2.0. It adds an ID token that tells the app who the user is, as checked by a provider such as Google or Okta.
A way to run a saga where one component tells each service what to do next and keeps the state of the whole flow.
A rough size in powers of ten. 300 and 700 have the same order of magnitude (hundreds); 300 and 30,000 do not.
Your own server that holds the real content. A CDN fetches from it when its cache has no fresh copy.
An extra cache layer between a CDN's edge locations and your origin server. Edges ask the shield, and only the shield asks the origin.
Changing data just before you show it, so the browser displays it as text and does not run it as code. HTML, JavaScript and URLs each need their own encoder.
Tuning a system so closely to one set of test cases that it scores well on them but does worse on new, real inputs.
Selling more units of a product than you have in stock, usually because two orders took the same last item.
Being the person responsible for a result, not just a task. The owner makes sure the work is finished, works in production and solves the real problem.
An extension of CAP. During a partition (P), choose availability (A) or consistency (C). Else (E), choose latency (L) or consistency (C).
One small chunk of data sent across a network, with a header that says where it comes from and where it goes. Big messages are split into many packets.
File data the Linux kernel keeps in RAM after a read or write. It makes repeated reads fast. Written data waits there before it goes to disk.
What a B-tree does when a new key does not fit in a full page: it moves some keys to a new page and adds a pointer in the parent page.
A SQL query with placeholders, like "WHERE id = ?", where the values are sent separately. The database never treats those values as code.
When some parts of a distributed system fail while other parts keep working. For example, one server or one network link breaks, and the rest of the system keeps running.
One piece of a dataset or stream that has been split up. Databases often call it a shard. In Kafka, a partition is one ordered log inside a topic.
A method that only calls another method with the same arguments and adds nothing. It is a sign of a shallow layer.
The result of running a password through a slow one-way function, such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt. The server stores only this, never the password, and cannot turn it back.
An older consensus algorithm by Leslie Lamport. A value is chosen in two phases, and each phase needs a majority of the servers.
Taking a card payment in two steps. Authorization holds the money on the card. Capture, done later, actually takes it. A hold expires if you wait too long.
A transfer from your balance at a payment processor to your own bank account, usually on a schedule. One payout can contain many payments, refunds and fees.
The security standard for any business that stores, processes or sends card data. The less card data touches your systems, the less of it applies to you.
In online shooters, a player who steps around a corner sees the enemy before the enemy sees them, because of network delay and buffering.
The value below which a given share of measurements fall. A p99 latency of 300 ms means 99% of requests took 300 ms or less.
A set of limits on numbers that affect speed, such as JavaScript size or LCP. Build tools can warn when a change goes over a limit.
A disaster recovery setup where data is copied to a second site all the time, but the app servers there stay off until you need them.
Sending the next request on a connection before the reply to the last one arrives, so you pay the round trip once for many requests, not once each.
An OAuth add-on where the app sends a hash of a random secret at the start and the secret itself at the end. A stolen authorization code is then useless without the secret.
A Claude Code mode where the agent reads files and proposes a plan, but does not change your source files.
The habit of underestimating the time, cost and risk of your own plans, because you think about the plan's details instead of how similar work really turned out.
Restoring a database to its exact state at a chosen moment, by loading a base backup and then replaying the saved change log up to that moment.
Walking a linked structure, such as a linked list or tree, where each step must load a node to find the address of the next one. The CPU cannot fetch ahead, so each step may wait for memory.
Using several kinds of databases in one system, each for the data it fits best. It adds running cost and data to keep in sync.
A SaaS design where tenants share the same resources. Cheap and simple to run, but needs tenant ids and limits to keep tenants apart.
A number that picks one program on a machine, such as 443 for a web server. An IP address finds the machine; the port finds the program.
In an inverted index, the list of documents (and often positions) that contain one term.
A written record of an incident after it ends. It covers the impact, what was done, the causes and the follow-up actions.
A load balancing rule that picks two servers at random and sends the request to the less busy one.
The column, or set of columns, that names each row of a table. No two rows may have the same value.
A standard JSON shape for API error bodies, defined in RFC 9457. It has fields such as type, title, status and detail, so clients can handle every error the same way.
A running program. Each process has its own private memory, its own open files and its own limits, so one process normally cannot read or damage another's memory.
The time on the clock of the machine that handles an event. It is simple and fast to use, but results change if events arrive late or a job catches up on a backlog.
The work of finding out what to build before you build it, for example by talking to users and testing ideas cheaply.
The person who decides what a team should build and why. They own whether customers want it and whether it works for the business.
A provider feature that saves the work done on a fixed start of a prompt and reuses it on later requests. It lowers cost and latency when the start is exactly the same.
An attack where text the model reads, such as a web page, file or issue, contains instructions that change what the model does.
Charging or crediting only part of a fixed fee because a plan was used for only part of a billing period, for example 20 of 30 days.
Publish/subscribe. Senders publish messages to a named topic or channel, and every subscriber of that topic gets a copy. Senders do not need to know who listens.
A proposed code change that others can read, comment on and approve before it is merged into the main branch. GitLab calls it a merge request.
Queries (or requests) per second. The usual way to say how much traffic a service gets.
The steps a database chooses to run a query, such as which index to use or whether to scan the whole table. EXPLAIN shows it.
A newer transport protocol that runs over UDP. It has reliable streams and built-in TLS, and a lost packet only blocks the streams it carried. HTTP/3 runs on it.
The smallest number of nodes that must answer before a read or write counts. With 3 copies, a common quorum is 2.
The most of something one customer may use, such as requests per second, storage or running jobs.
A bug where the result depends on the timing of threads. Two threads touch the same data at about the same time, and one change can be lost.
A numbered period of time in Raft. Each term starts with an election and has at most one leader. A higher term always wins.
A consensus algorithm. One elected leader copies its log of changes to the other servers, and a change counts once a majority has stored it. etcd and Consul use it.
Retrieval-augmented generation. The app first searches your own documents for text that matches the question, then gives that text to the model so it can answer from it.
A rule that caps how many requests a client may make in a period of time, and rejects the extra ones.
A second step after search. A separate model scores the top results again, and only the best few go to the language model.
How many places, such as pages or files, a storage engine must check to answer one read.
An isolation level where you only see data that other transactions have committed. Each statement can see newer data than the last.
A copy of data shaped for one kind of read, such as a feed table or search index. It is built from the main data and updated after each change.
A caching pattern where the app only talks to the cache, and the cache loads missing data from the database itself.
A lock that lets many readers in at the same time, or one writer alone. It helps when data is read often and changed rarely.
A promise that after you save something, your own later reads will show it, even if other users see it a bit later.
Measuring performance in the browsers of your real visitors and sending the numbers to your own analytics.
Moving data or work between machines so each one has a fair share, for example after you add a machine.
A search metric. Of the documents that should be found for a question, the share that appear in the top k results.
A simple way to merge several ranked result lists. Each document gets 1 / (k + rank) points from each list, and the points are added up. It needs no tuning.
A difference found during reconciliation, such as a payment that is on only one side, a wrong amount or a duplicate. Each one needs a type, an owner and a fix.
Regularly comparing your own records with outside records, like bank statements, and explaining every difference.
The most data you accept to lose in a disaster, measured as time. An RPO of 5 minutes means you may lose up to the last 5 minutes of writes.
The longest you accept a service to be down after a disaster before it works again. An RTO of 1 hour means you must be back within an hour.
The DNS server your app asks. It walks the DNS tree for you, from the root down, and caches the answers it gets.
A checklist for services: rate (requests per second), errors (how many fail) and duration (how long they take).
Estimating from how a group of similar past projects really turned out, then adjusting for clear differences. It is a way of taking the "outside view".
A longer-lived token that an app uses only to get new short-lived access tokens. The server can revoke it to end the login.
A file the browser must load and process before it can show the page, such as CSS or a normal script tag in the head.
A full copy of a database that runs on another machine and is kept up to date with the original.
Several servers that run the same commands in the same order from a shared log, so they all end up with the same state.
How far a follower is behind the leader. A write on the leader is not yet visible on a follower during this time.
Letting only one request load a missing key, while other requests for the same key wait and share its answer.
An HTTP header that tells the client how long to wait, in seconds or until a date, before it sends the next request.
When retries turn one request into many calls. They multiply when several layers each retry. Three layers that each try 4 times can send 64 calls to the bottom layer.
A limit on how many retries a client may send, such as retries under 10% of its requests. When the budget is used up, the client fails the request instead of retrying.
Sending the same request again after it failed or timed out.
New ledger entries with the same amounts and opposite signs, used to cancel wrong entries without editing or deleting them.
Short for "request for comments". A written proposal shared so that others can comment before a decision is made. Many companies use it as another name for a design doc with a formal review.
Fixing a bad release by shipping a new fix, not by going back to the old version.
Each player's game guesses the other player's inputs and keeps running. When the real inputs differ, it goes back and re-runs the game from that point.
Undoing a deploy or config change by going back to the last version that worked.
A deploy that replaces old servers or pods with new ones a few at a time. For a while, old and new versions run side by side.
The deeper reason a problem happened, not just its visible symptom. Big incidents often have several contributing causes.
A DNS server at the top of the name tree. It does not know final answers. It tells resolvers which servers handle .com, .org and other top-level domains.
A load balancing rule that gives each server the next request in turn, without looking at how busy it is.
The time for a message to go from your computer to the server and for the answer to come back. Games often call it ping.
A database feature that adds a filter, such as "only this tenant's rows", to every query on a table, so one missed WHERE clause cannot leak data. Superusers, and usually table owners, skip it.
A lock on one database row. Other transactions that want to change or lock that row wait until the holder commits or rolls back.
A written list of rules for grading an answer, such as what a strong interview answer must show, or that an AI reply "must mention the refund deadline".
A file of standing instructions that a coding tool loads into the agent's context, such as Cursor rules or Copilot instructions. It guides the agent but does not enforce anything.
A short written guide for one alert or task. It says what the problem means, how to check it and what steps fix it.
A chain of small local transactions across services. If a later step fails, earlier steps are undone by compensating transactions.
A random value added to each password before hashing, so two users with the same password get different hashes. Good libraries create and store it for you.
In Flink, a checkpoint you trigger by hand. You use it to stop a job, deploy new code or change parallelism, then resume from the same state.
A way to give feedback in three parts. Name the situation, describe the behaviour you saw, and say what impact it had. It avoids judging the person.
A list of every component and version inside your software, including dependencies of dependencies. It tells you fast whether a newly found flaw affects you.
Sending one query to every shard and merging the answers. It is as slow as the slowest shard.
The database does not force a structure on writes. The code that reads the data decides what it means, and must handle old and new shapes.
The database checks every write against a fixed schema, such as a SQL table definition, and rejects data that does not fit.
What a piece of work covers. In a project, it is the list of features that are in or out. In a career, it is the size of the work you own, from one task up to work across many teams.
The person in an incident who writes down what happens, with the time, such as each decision, change and status update.
An extra index that lets you find rows by a field other than the main key, such as orders by customer ID.
A service that stores passwords, keys and tokens, controls who may read them, and hands them to apps at run time, so they never sit in code.
Everyone sees all operations in the same order, and each client's own order is kept. The order may lag behind real time.
The strictest isolation level. The result is the same as if the transactions had run one after another.
When an old server state arrives, the client resets to it and replays the inputs the server has not processed yet, so the player does not jump back.
A web standard where the browser opens one long HTTP response and the server keeps writing events into it. Data flows one way, from server to client.
Building a page's HTML on the server for each request, so the browser gets content instead of an empty page and a large script.
How one service finds the current network addresses of another service, while servers start, stop and move.
A layer of proxies, often one next to each service, that handles traffic between services, such as retries, mutual TLS and metrics, without changes to app code.
A shared list of running service instances and their addresses, kept current by health checks. Consul is a common example.
A window that groups the events of one key, such as one user, and closes after a gap with no events, for example 30 minutes. Its length depends on the data.
The step, often days after a payment, when banks actually move the money to the processor or merchant.
A number that says how bad an incident is, often SEV-1 for the worst. It decides who gets paged and how fast the team must act.
A module whose interface is complex, or that does little work. Calling it is not much easier than writing its code yourself.
The field, such as a user ID, that decides which shard a record lives on.
One piece of a large dataset that has been split across machines. Each shard holds a different part of the data.
One count split across many rows. Each write adds to a random row, so no single row gets all the writes. To read the total, you add up all the rows.
Giving each customer a random small set of workers, so two customers rarely share the exact same set and one bad customer fully hurts very few others.
An extra output stream from a stream processing step. Flink can send events that arrive too late for their window there, so they are not lost silently.
A SaaS design where a tenant gets its own resources, such as its own database or full stack. Strong isolation, higher cost.
One part that, if it fails, stops the whole system. You remove it by running more than one copy and making sure they do not all fail together.
The "S" in SOLID. A module should have one reason to change, meaning one group of people who ask for its changes. It does not mean "one method per class".
A class that allows only one instance and gives global access to it, often through getInstance(). Used as global state, it hides dependencies and can leak state between tests.
Service level agreement. A contract with customers that promises a level of service and has a penalty if it is missed.
Service level indicator. A measure of how well a service works for users, often good events divided by valid events.
A rate limit that counts requests in the last N seconds, measured from now, so there is no reset edge to exploit.
Service level objective. A target for an SLI over a time window, such as 99.9% of requests succeed over 4 weeks.
An informal name for a package confusion attack where someone publishes a real, harmful package under a name that AI models tend to invent, and waits for AI-written code to install it.
An isolation level where a transaction reads from one frozen view of the database, taken at its first statement.
A TLS extension where the client sends the host name it wants in its first message, so one IP address can serve many sites with different certificates.
A 64-bit ID built from a timestamp, a machine number and a counter, first made by Twitter. IDs from one machine sort by time.
How much disk a storage engine uses compared with the size of the live data, for example because of old versions.
One step inside a trace, such as one call to a database, with its start time and duration.
A very simple program that explores one hard technical or design question and ignores everything else. It is usually thrown away. It reduces risk or makes an estimate more reliable.
A failure where two nodes both think they are the leader and both accept writes. The two copies then disagree.
Using your own influence to create chances for someone else, such as naming them for a lead role or crediting their work in public. It is more than giving advice.
An attack where user input changes the meaning of a SQL query, because the code glued the input into the query text. Parameterized queries stop it.
A DNS record that says where a service runs, as a host name and a port, with a priority and a weight for choosing between hosts.
An attack that tricks your server into sending requests to places the attacker picks, such as internal services or a cloud metadata address.
A sorted file on disk that an LSM-tree writes once and never changes. New data goes into new SSTables.
The list of function calls that were running when an error happened, printed with the error. It shows where in the code the error came from.
A level above senior on the technical (non-manager) path at many companies. A staff engineer often sets technical direction for problems that cross many teams.
Releasing a change to a growing share of servers or users in steps, checking health at each step before the next.
Serving an expired cached value for a short time while one request fetches a fresh copy in the background.
A way to tell a story about past work in four parts: Situation, Task, Action and Result. Companies such as Amazon and Google suggest it for behavioural interviews.
A thread never gets the lock or resource it waits for, because other threads always get it first.
The part of a stream processor that stores its state. In Flink, the default keeps state in memory on the Java heap; the RocksDB backend keeps it on local disk.

A model where a thing is always in exactly one named state, and only listed moves (transitions) can change that state. For example, an order can go from confirmed to shipped, but not from cancelled to shipped.
A stateless server keeps no user data in its own memory between requests. Any server can handle any request, so you can add or remove servers easily.
A web page where a company tells users whether its services work, and posts updates during an incident.
Cutting a word to a root form, so "running" and "run" or "foxes" and "fox" match the same search term.
A load balancer setting that sends every request from one user to the same server, often using a cookie.
Stock held for one buyer for a short time, for example during checkout. It is released if the buyer does not pay in time.
A very common word, like "the" or "for", that a search engine often drops because it does not help find documents.
A short list of true stories from your past work, prepared before interviews. Each story is linked to the themes it can answer, such as conflict or failure.
A way to replace an old system bit by bit. You build new parts next to it and move behaviour across one piece at a time, instead of one big rewrite.
A design pattern that puts each variant of one decision, such as how to price an order, behind the same shape so you can swap them. In modern languages it is often just a function you pass in.
Work that is a little above someone's current level, given on purpose so they can grow. It works best with clear goals and a way to undo mistakes.
An interview where every candidate for a role gets the same planned questions, and answers are scored against the same written rubric.
A model feature that forces the reply to match a JSON schema you give. It controls the shape of the data, not whether the values are true.
A helper agent that works in its own, separate context and sends back only a short summary.
A ledger account where you put money you cannot explain yet, so it is not lost or counted as income. Someone owns each item and moves it out once it is explained.
The leader waits until a follower confirms it has the change before it tells the client the write is done.
A request from your program to the kernel, such as read, write or open. The CPU switches into kernel mode to do it, which costs time.
The fixed instructions an app sends to a model with every request, such as its role, rules and output format. It is not a secret and not a security control.
When a schema change makes the database copy every row of a table, and often rebuild its indexes. On a big table this can take a long time and lock it.
The latency of the slowest requests, such as the p99 or p99.9. It is what your unluckiest users feel.
The transport protocol most of the internet uses. It opens a connection and delivers bytes reliably and in order, sending lost data again.
Weak spots in code or design that make future changes to that code slower. The extra effort is the "interest"; cleaning up is paying back the debt.
A request setting that controls how random a model's word choice is. Higher gives more varied text. Lower sticks to the most likely words, but output can still vary.
A design pattern where a base class fixes the order of steps and subclasses fill in the steps that differ. Passing the changing step in as a function is often simpler.
One customer organisation, such as one company, in a system that serves many customers. Its data and load must stay separate from other tenants.
A fake object that stands in for a real one in a test, such as a fake payment service that always says "paid".
A picture of a healthy test suite. Many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests, and a few slow end-to-end tests at the top.
The rules a search engine uses to turn text into terms, for example split into words, lowercase them and cut them to a root form. Documents and queries must use the same rules.
A way to score search matches. A term counts more if it appears often in the document and appears in few documents overall.
One line of execution inside a process. Threads of one process share its memory and open files, but each thread has its own stack.
An extra check during a card payment, where the card's bank asks the customer to prove it is them, for example with a one-time code.
Keep 3 copies of important data (1 primary and 2 backups), on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy in another place.
How TCP opens a connection. The client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. It costs one round trip before any data moves.
How many times per second a game server updates the world. Each update is one tick. A 15 ms tick means about 66 ticks per second.
A small database server whose only job is to hand out unique numbers, for example for primary keys in a sharded system.
A unique column, such as the id, added at the end of a sort order. When two rows have the same value, it decides which comes first, so the order never changes.
Sending a request to two servers at once; the first server to start work on it tells the other to cancel.
A price plan where the unit price changes with volume. In the graduated form, each tier's units are charged at that tier's price.
A database built for timestamped data points, like metrics or sensor readings. It makes writes and time-range queries cheap.
The time from the start of a page request until the first byte of the response arrives. It includes redirects, DNS, the connection, TLS and the server's work.
How long a model takes to send the first token of its reply after it gets the request. It is how long a user waits before any text appears.
A time limit for waiting. If no answer comes back in time, the caller stops waiting.
Ending the encrypted TLS connection at a proxy or gateway. The proxy decrypts the request, can inspect it, and then forwards it, ideally over a new TLS connection.

Transport Layer Security. A protocol that encrypts data on a connection, detects changes to it, and lets the client check the server's identity with a certificate. The server can also ask the client for one. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.
A rate limit where each request takes a token from a bucket that refills at a fixed rate. The bucket size sets the biggest burst.
Splitting text into small pieces, usually words, before they are cleaned and indexed for search.
A marker that says a key was deleted. Stores that never change old files write it instead of removing data, and clean it up later.
A model feature where the model asks your app to run a function, with arguments in a fixed format. Your code runs it and sends the result back.
The last part of a domain name, like .com or .org. Its name servers know which servers hold each domain under it.
A lab metric: the total time after First Contentful Paint when long tasks block the main thread. Only the part of each task over 50 ms counts. It helps find INP problems but does not replace INP.
A record of the path one request takes through many services, with the timing of each step.
A group of database reads and writes that succeed or fail as one unit.
A table where a service saves outgoing events in the same transaction as its data. A separate relay then publishes them.
An error that may go away on its own in a moment, such as a busy service or a dropped connection. These are the errors worth retrying.
Google's clock API used by Spanner. It returns a time interval that is sure to contain the true time, instead of a single time.
A way of working where every developer merges small changes into one shared branch (trunk or main) at least daily, instead of keeping long-lived branches.
A point where data enters your code from a source you do not control, such as a user, a partner or another team's service. Data should be checked there.
The set of root certificates that an operating system, browser or runtime trusts. A certificate chain must end at one of them.
Time to live. How long a stored value, such as a cache entry, a lock or a seat hold, lives before it expires.
A time window of fixed size that does not overlap with the next one, like each minute. Every event belongs to exactly one tumbling window.
A way to commit across several databases. A coordinator asks every one to prepare, then tells all of them to commit or roll back.
A decision you can easily undo if it turns out wrong. It should be made quickly, by a small group, with a light process.
A simple transport protocol that sends single messages with no connection. It does not promise that messages arrive, arrive once, or arrive in order.
A 128-bit ID with a millisecond timestamp first and random bits after it. It is written as 26 characters that sort in time order.
A test of one small piece of code, such as a function or a class, on its own. It runs fast, often in milliseconds.
Charging customers for what they actually use, such as API calls, messages or tokens, instead of only a fixed monthly fee.
A checklist for resources like CPU, memory and disks: utilization (how busy), saturation (extra work it cannot handle yet, often queued) and errors.
The restricted CPU mode your code runs in. It cannot do I/O or run privileged instructions. For that it asks the kernel, which runs in kernel mode with full access.
How busy a resource is, as a share of its capacity. A server at 90% utilization is busy 9 tenths of the time.
A 128-bit ID that any server can create on its own, with almost no chance of a clash. It is usually written as 36 letters, digits and dashes.
A list of (node, counter) pairs kept with each version of data. Comparing two lists shows whether one version came from the other, or whether they are in conflict.
A database that finds the stored vectors nearest to a given one, for example to find similar texts. pgvector adds this to Postgres.
Handling more load by moving to a bigger machine, with more CPU and memory. Simple, but there is a largest machine, and it is still one machine.
One of many points that a single server owns on a consistent hash ring. Many small points spread keys more evenly than one big one.
A queue page in front of a site. It lets visitors in at a rate the site can handle and shows the others their wait.
In Amazon SQS, how long a received message stays hidden from other workers. If it is not deleted in that time, it comes back.
The clock that shows the real date and time. It can jump when someone sets it, and NTP changes its speed, so it is unsafe for measuring how long something takes.
A disaster recovery (DR) strategy where a smaller but working copy of production always runs at a second site, ready to scale up and take traffic.
In stream processing, a marker that says event time has reached a given point. It tells the engine when a window can be closed. An event whose time is already behind the watermark is late.
An HTTP request that a server sends to your endpoint when an event happens, so you do not have to keep asking for changes.
A protocol that starts as an HTTP request and then keeps one connection open, so the client and the server can both send messages at any time.
A database that splits tables into partitions by key and spreads them over many nodes, such as Cassandra. Fast queries must give the partition key.
A log where a database records every change before it applies it, so it can recover after a crash. CDC tools read it.
How many bytes a storage engine writes to disk for each byte your app writes. Higher means more background disk work.
A caching pattern where writes go to the cache first and reach the database later. Fast, but data can be lost if the cache fails.
A bug where two transactions read the same data, then each writes a different row. Each write is fine alone, but together they break a rule.
A caching pattern where every write goes to the cache and the database together, so the cache stays fresh.
An attack where someone gets their JavaScript to run on your site in another user's browser. It can then read the page and act as that user.
An arrangement with an LLM provider where it does not store your prompts and replies after it sends the response. It is usually set up by request, not on by default.
A TLS 1.3 option where a returning client sends data in its first message. It saves a round trip, but an attacker can replay that data.
